claim: Calcium signals were recorded from projection neurons in the honey bee antennal lobe at high temporal resolution using fast calcium imaging.
source: Here, we used fast calcium imaging to track the activity of projection neurons in the honey bee antennal lobe (AL) during olfactory stimulation at high temporal resolution.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the use of fast calcium imaging to record projection neuron activity at high temporal resolution.

claim: Projection neurons exhibit heterogeneous response profiles during olfactory stimulation.
source: We observed a heterogeneity of response profiles and an abundance of inhibitory activities, resulting in various response latencies and stimulus-specific post-odour neural signatures.
evidence: The abstract describes observed heterogeneity in response profiles based on experimental data.

claim: Inhibitory activities are abundant in projection neuron responses.
source: We observed a heterogeneity of response profiles and an abundance of inhibitory activities, resulting in various response latencies and stimulus-specific post-odour neural signatures.
evidence: The abstract explicitly mentions abundance of inhibitory activities observed in the data.

claim: A mushroom body model was constructed implementing fundamental features of connectivity between olfactory projection neurons, Kenyon cells, and MB output neurons.
source: Recorded calcium signals were fed to a mushroom body (MB) model constructed implementing the fundamental features of connectivity between olfactory projection neurons, Kenyon cells (KC), and MB output neurons (MBON).
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the construction of an MB model with specific connectivity features.

claim: The mushroom body model accounts for increased odorant discrimination in the MB compared to the AL.
source: The model accounts for the increase of odorant discrimination in the MB compared to the AL and reveals the recruitment of two distinct KC populations that represent odorants and their aftersmell as two separate but temporally coherent neural objects.
evidence: The abstract states that the model accounts for increased discrimination, based on modeling results.

claim: Two distinct Kenyon cell populations are recruited that represent odorants and their aftersmell as separate but temporally coherent neural objects.
source: The model accounts for the increase of odorant discrimination in the MB compared to the AL and reveals the recruitment of two distinct KC populations that represent odorants and their aftersmell as two separate but temporally coherent neural objects.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the recruitment of two distinct KC populations based on model results.

claim: Learning-induced modulation of KC-to-MBON synapses can explain variations in associative learning scores across different conditioning protocols.
source: Finally, we showed that the learning-induced modulation of KC-to-MBON synapses can explain both the variations in associative learning scores across different conditioning protocols used in bees and the bees' response latency.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that synaptic modulation explains learning score variations.

claim: Learning-induced modulation of KC-to-MBON synapses can explain bees' response latency.
source: Finally, we showed that the learning-induced modulation of KC-to-MBON synapses can explain both the variations in associative learning scores across different conditioning protocols used in bees and the bees' response latency.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that synaptic modulation explains response latency.

claim: The model provides an explanation of how time contingency between stimulus and reward can be encoded without the need for time tracking.
source: Thus, it provides a simple explanation of how the time contingency between the stimulus and the reward can be encoded without the need for time tracking.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a conclusion from the modeling work.

claim: Honey bees have been used extensively to study olfactory perception and learning.
source: Among them, the honey bee Apis mellifera has played a pivotal role in our understanding of these processes due to its behavioural accessibility and tractability of its nervous system.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The proboscis extension reflex (PER) is used to investigate olfactory perception and learning in bees.
source: In bees, olfactory perception and learning have been typically investigated using the proboscis extension reflex (PER; Giurfa, 2007; Menzel, 1999), a protocol that relies on pairing a neutral olfactory stimulus (the conditioned stimulus or CS) with a positive reinforcement of sugar solution (the unconditioned stimulus or US) (Bitterman et al., 1983; Giurfa and Sandoz, 2012; Takeda, 1961).
evidence: The introduction describes PER as a standard method, supported by citations.

claim: In classical PER conditioning, the CS precedes and partially overlaps US presentation, resulting in high levels of specific memory.
source: In the classical version of PER conditioning, the CS precedes and partially overlaps US presentation. This results in high levels of specific memory for the conditioned odorant.
evidence: The introduction describes this as an established protocol characteristic.

claim: Backward conditioning (reward precedes stimulus) does not establish positive association in honey bees.
source: Conversely, when the reward precedes the stimulus (backward conditioning), no positive association can be established (Felsenberg et al., 2014; Hellstern et al., 1998).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies showing this behavioral result.

claim: Olfactory sensory neurons expressing the same olfactory receptor converge onto one of ~160 glomeruli in the honey bee antennal lobe.
source: Olfactory sensory neurons innervate the first olfactory processing centre, the antennal lobe (AL), where the neurons expressing the same olfactory receptor converge onto one of ~160 glomeruli, the anatomical and functional units of the AL (Flanagan and Mercer, 1989).
evidence: The introduction states this neuroanatomical fact with citation.

claim: Approximately 800 projection neurons forward signals from the antennal lobe to higher order brain centres.
source: The signal processed in the AL is forwarded by ~800 output neurons – the projection neurons (PNs) – to higher order brain centres: the mushroom bodies (MBs), central, paired structures dedicated to multisensory integration, memory storage and retrieval (Heisenberg, 2003; Stopfer, 2014), and the lateral horn of the protocerebrum, a diffuse bilateral structure involved in valence coding of odorants (Jeanne et al., 2018; Roussel et al., 2014; Strutz et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction provides this neuroanatomical detail with citations.

claim: The mushroom body contains approximately 185,000 Kenyon cells in honey bees.
source: The MB architecture is defined by the layout of its ~185,000 intrinsic neurons, the Kenyon cells (KCs).
evidence: The introduction states this neuroanatomical fact.

claim: Each Kenyon cell receives input from multiple projection neurons.
source: Each KC extends its dendritic arborisation within the MB input regions, termed the calyces, where it receives input from multiple PNs, and projects its axon to the MB output region, termed the pedunculus, where it bifurcates into the vertical (α and γ) and the medial (β) lobes (Mobbs, 1982; Strausfeld, 2002).
evidence: The introduction describes this connectivity pattern with citations.

claim: GABAergic feedback neurons play a critical role in maintaining sparse output in Kenyon cells.
source: Kenyon cells integrate, among others, the excitatory input of olfactory PNs and the inhibitory input of recurrent GABAergic feedback neurons (Ganeshina and Menzel, 2001; Grünewald, 1999; Rybak and Menzel, 1993; Zwaka et al., 2018). The latter plays a critical role in shaping KCs olfactory responsiveness and maintaining a sparse output over a wide range of odorants and concentrations (Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Stopfer, 2014).
evidence: The introduction describes this functional role with citations.

claim: The VUMmx1 neuron is an unpaired octopaminergic neuron that conveys appetitive reward-related information.
source: Antennal lobe, mushroom body and lateral horn are innervated by the VUMmx1 neuron (Hammer, 1993), an unpaired octopaminergic neuron conveying appetitive reward-related information to the olfactory circuit and mediating reward-based olfactory memory formation.
evidence: The introduction describes this neuron's function with citation.

claim: Each odorant is represented with a specific pattern of excitatory and inhibitory responses across glomeruli in the antennal lobe.
source: In vivo imaging allowed observing that each stimulus is represented with a specific pattern of excitatory and inhibitory responses across the glomeruli of the AL (Galizia et al., 1999; Sachse and Galizia, 2002; Sachse et al., 1999), and that perceptually similar odorants elicit similar glomerular response patterns (Guerrieri et al., 2005).
evidence: The introduction cites previous imaging studies showing this pattern.

claim: Calcium imaging of AL activity has typically been conducted at low temporal resolutions (~100–200ms).
source: Calcium imaging of AL activity has been typically conducted at low temporal resolutions (~100–200ms; Locatelli et al., 2016; Mertes et al., 2021; Nouvian et al., 2018; Sachse and Galizia, 2003).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies with their temporal resolution specifications.

claim: Calcium signal onset is fast (<10ms) while decay is relatively slow (>100ms).
source: While calcium signal decay is relatively slow (>100ms), its onset is fast (<10ms) (Helassa et al., 2015; Moreaux and Laurent, 2007), and provides the possibility for investigating parameters such as glomerular response latency (Junek et al., 2010; Paoli et al., 2018a), signal frequency components (Paoli et al., 2016) and interglomerular information transfer (Chen et al., 2023; Paoli et al., 2023b).
evidence: The introduction cites studies characterizing calcium signal dynamics.

claim: The temporal resolution of calcium imaging recordings was significantly improved to <10 ms using a resonant scanning multiphoton microscope.
source: In this study, we significantly improved the temporal resolution of calcium imaging recordings of olfactory neurons in the bee brain by means of a resonant scanning multiphoton microscope. This allowed us to record calcium activity at a<10 ms resolution, preserving temporal information of the olfactory code and yielding a more realistic representation of odour trajectories in the AL.
evidence: The introduction describes the methodological improvement achieved in this study.

claim: Most glomerular response profiles presented an inhibitory component.
source: First, we observed that odour representation changes dynamically during and after an olfactory stimulation, resulting in specific odour and after-odour images. Then, we showed that most glomerular response profiles presented an inhibitory component, suggesting that glomerular activity is strongly shaped by local inhibition, with only a minor influence – if any – of local excitatory interneurons.
evidence: The introduction summarizes findings from the study's data analysis.

claim: Glomerular activity is strongly shaped by local inhibition with only minor influence of local excitatory interneurons.
source: Then, we showed that most glomerular response profiles presented an inhibitory component, suggesting that glomerular activity is strongly shaped by local inhibition, with only a minor influence – if any – of local excitatory interneurons.
evidence: The introduction presents this as an inference from the observed inhibitory components.

claim: Kenyon cells exhibit phasic and sparse activity.
source: Electrophysiology experiments have provided insight on the phasic and sparse activity of Kenyon cells as well as into its oscillatory nature (Laurent and Davidowitz, 1994; Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Stopfer, 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites electrophysiology studies characterizing KC activity.

claim: Less than 20% of Kenyon cells are active upon olfactory stimulation, and only ~5% are stimulus-specific.
source: Second, recurrent inhibitory neurons such as the A3 feedback neurons in the bee (Mobbs, 1982; Rybak and Menzel, 1993; Szyszka et al., 2005; Zwaka et al., 2018), the APL neuron in fly (Lin et al., 2014), and the giant GABAergic neuron in the locust (Papadopoulou et al., 2011), modulate MB KCs firing rate so that less than 20% of KCs are active upon olfactory stimulation, and only ~5% are stimulus-specific (Honegger et al., 2011; Turner et al., 2008).
evidence: The introduction cites studies showing KC sparseness levels.

claim: Mushroom bodies have a 20 Hz oscillatory cycle in bees and locusts.
source: Third, as in bees and locusts, MB have a 20 Hz oscillatory cycle (Cassenaer and Laurent, 2007; Laurent and Naraghi, 1994; Popov and Szyszka, 2020), we fed the model with experimentally recorded calcium signals resampled at a 20 Hz-sampling frequency.
evidence: The introduction cites studies showing the oscillatory frequency of MBs.

claim: Projection neurons of eight bees were back-filled with the calcium sensor Fura-2.
source: Antennal lobe PNs of eight bees were back-filled with the calcium sensor Fura-2 (Paoli and Haase, 2018b; Sachse and Galizia, 2002) to measure odour-induced glomerular activity of (~25 glomeruli/AL) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The Results section describes the experimental procedure performed.

claim: Approximately 25 glomeruli per antennal lobe were measured.
source: Antennal lobe PNs of eight bees were back-filled with the calcium sensor Fura-2 (Paoli and Haase, 2018b; Sachse and Galizia, 2002) to measure odour-induced glomerular activity of (~25 glomeruli/AL) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The Results section states the number of glomeruli measured.

claim: Calcium signals were recorded upon stimulation with 1-hexanol, 1-heptanol, and peppermint oil.
source: Calcium signal was recorded upon stimulation with two monomolecular odorants (1-hexanol, 1-heptanol) and a complex fragrance (peppermint oil) on a 5 s/25 s ON/OFF conformation for 20 trials (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: The Results section describes the odorants used in the experiments.

claim: Odorants were presented for 5 seconds with 25 second intervals for 20 trials.
source: Calcium signal was recorded upon stimulation with two monomolecular odorants (1-hexanol, 1-heptanol) and a complex fragrance (peppermint oil) on a 5 s/25 s ON/OFF conformation for 20 trials (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: The Results section describes the stimulation protocol.

claim: Fast calcium imaging revealed high variability of odorant-elicited glomerular response profiles.
source: Fast calcium imaging revealed the high variability of odorant-elicited glomerular response profiles.
evidence: The Results section states this observation from the imaging data.

claim: Across-trial correlation is elevated during odour arrival and remains around 0.5 seconds after stimulus termination.
source: Figure 1E, E' show that across-trial correlation is elevated during odour arrival and remains around 0.5seconds after stimulus termination.
evidence: The Results section describes correlation analysis shown in Figure 1E, E'.

claim: Odour coding was stable throughout the entire imaging period in the experimental conditions used.
source: This shows that, in our experimental conditions, odour coding was stable throughout the entire imaging period.
evidence: The Results section concludes this from the correlation analysis.

claim: 48% of all recorded glomerular traces were excitatory, 37% inhibitory, and 15% unresponsive.
source: Of all traces, 48% were excitatory, 37% inhibitory, and 15% unresponsive (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative breakdown of response types from the data.

claim: 46% of glomerular responses (251 out of 546) displayed an inhibitory component either during or after olfactory stimulation.
source: Moreover, 251 glomerular responses out of 546 (46%) displayed an inhibitory component either during or after olfactory stimulation.
evidence: The Results section provides this quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Excitatory responses have a mean onset latency of 313±22ms.
source: Figure 2E shows that excitatory responses (groups 4–8) all share a similar onset (313±22ms, n=263), which is shorter than that of inhibitory profiles (groups 1–3; 351±47ms, n=201) (Kruskal-Wallis test, p<0.05, Tukey-Kramer multiple comparison correction).
evidence: The Results section reports measured latencies with statistical analysis.

claim: Inhibitory responses have a mean onset latency of 351±47ms, which is longer than excitatory responses.
source: Figure 2E shows that excitatory responses (groups 4–8) all share a similar onset (313±22ms, n=263), which is shorter than that of inhibitory profiles (groups 1–3; 351±47ms, n=201) (Kruskal-Wallis test, p<0.05, Tukey-Kramer multiple comparison correction).
evidence: The Results section reports measured latencies with statistical comparison.

claim: The latency of short excitatory responses' termination (346±47ms) is coherent with the onset of inhibitory profiles.
source: Moreover, the latency of short excitatory responses' termination (groups 7 and 8; 346±47ms, n=60) is coherent with the onset of inhibitory profiles.
evidence: The Results section reports this temporal relationship from the data.

claim: Odour representation in the antennal lobe is shaped initially by excitatory input from OSNs and reshaped approximately 40ms later by local inhibition.
source: These findings indicate that odour representation in the AL is shaped initially by the excitatory input delivered by the OSNs and reshaped – approximately 40ms later – by local inhibition.
evidence: The Results section infers this temporal sequence from the latency measurements.

claim: Olfactory tuning in honey bees differs from Drosophila, where both excitatory and inhibitory local neurons contribute to molding the neural correlate of olfactory input.
source: Such an olfactory tuning is different from what is proposed in Drosophila, where both excitatory and inhibitory local neurons contribute to moulding the neural correlate of an olfactory input (Chou et al., 2010; Olsen et al., 2007).
evidence: The Results section compares findings to cited Drosophila studies.

claim: In the MB model, approximately 25 projection neurons diverge onto 1000 Kenyon cells, with each KC innervated by approximately 8 PNs.
source: Thus, we generated a MB network where ~ 25 PNs (i.e., the average number of glomeruli imaged during a calcium imaging experiment) diverge onto 1000 KCs, with each KC being innervated by ~8 PNs.
evidence: The Results section describes the model architecture parameters.

claim: The model implements winner-takes-it-all feedback inhibition by forcing only 10% of KCs receiving the largest summed input to generate an action potential.
source: Hence, we enriched the model with a winner-takes-it-all feedback inhibition mechanism by forcing that only 10% of KCs receiving the largest summed input generate an action potential.
evidence: The Results section describes this model implementation rule.

claim: The model was fed with experimentally recorded calcium signals resampled at 20 Hz sampling frequency.
source: Third, as in bees and locusts, MB have a 20 Hz oscillatory cycle (Cassenaer and Laurent, 2007; Laurent and Naraghi, 1994; Popov and Szyszka, 2020), we fed the model with experimentally recorded calcium signals resampled at a 20 Hz-sampling frequency.
evidence: The Results section describes the input data processing for the model.

claim: Before odorant onset, the KC population varies randomly between adjacent time points with a turnover rate of approximately 61%.
source: The analysis of KC population turnover (Figure 4B) showed that, before odorant onset, the population varies randomly between adjacent time points while it stabilises during olfactory stimulation, with a turnover rate of ~10%.
evidence: The Results section reports turnover rates from model simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: During olfactory stimulation, KC population stabilizes with a turnover rate of approximately 10%.
source: The analysis of KC population turnover (Figure 4B) showed that, before odorant onset, the population varies randomly between adjacent time points while it stabilises during olfactory stimulation, with a turnover rate of ~10%.
evidence: The Results section reports turnover rates from model simulations.

claim: Two odorant-specific sets of Kenyon cells are recruited during olfactory stimulation: one at stimulus onset and one at odour termination.
source: The dynamics of KC recruitment across bees and odorants (Figure 4C) indicates that two odorant-specific sets of cells are recruited during an olfactory stimulation: the first one at stimulus onset, the second one at odour termination (see Figure 4C, t=5 s).
evidence: The Results section describes KC recruitment patterns from model simulations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Both KC populations recruited at onset and offset are stable with turnover rates below pre-stimulus baseline for up to 15 seconds after stimulus offset.
source: Both populations are rather stable, with a turnover rate below the pre-stimulus baseline for up to 15 s after stimulus offset (turnover ratepre-stim=0.61 ± 0.14; turnover rateON_0-5s=0.17 ± 0.05; turnover rateOFF_5-10s=0.25 ± 0.04; turnover rateOFF_10-15s=0.33 ± 0.08).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative turnover rate measurements from model simulations.

claim: Neural activity shows high correlation across time points during olfactory stimulation and during the post-odour window in both PN and KC populations.
source: Correlation analysis of stimulus-induced responses (Figure 5D and E) showed a high correlation of neural activity across time points during olfactory stimulation and during the post-odour window both in the recorded PN population and in the simulated KCs.
evidence: The Results section describes correlation analysis results shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Across-odorants correlation is high in the PN space (r=0.4) but proximal to zero in the KC space.
source: Furthermore, the across-odorants correlation is rather high in the PN space (Pearson's correlation coefficient, r=0.4), but proximal to zero in the KC space, supporting the notion that the MB network increases stimulus discriminability, not only during but also after odour offset.
evidence: The Results section reports correlation coefficients from the analysis.

claim: The MB network increases stimulus discriminability during and after odour offset.
source: Furthermore, the across-odorants correlation is rather high in the PN space (Pearson's correlation coefficient, r=0.4), but proximal to zero in the KC space, supporting the notion that the MB network increases stimulus discriminability, not only during but also after odour offset.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the correlation differences between PN and KC spaces.

claim: Odorants are better separated from each other and remain separated for a longer time in the KC space compared to the PN space.
source: However, the principal component analysis showed that odorants are better separated from each other and that they remained separated for a longer time in the KC space compared to the PN space.
evidence: The Results section describes PCA results comparing PN and KC spaces.

claim: Response vectors calculated from PN data were highly correlated (r=0.71 ± 0.08).
source: Notably, while response vectors calculated from PN data were highly correlated (r=0.71 ± 0.08), such a correlation significantly decreased in the modelled KC space (r=0.52 ± 0.10; Student's t-test between r distributions of PN and KC data: p 0, n=4774), indicating that the signal transformation operated by the proposed MB neural architecture induces a strong decorrelation among odour signatures.
evidence: The Results section reports correlation values from analysis of simulated odorant profiles.

claim: Correlation significantly decreased in the modelled KC space (r=0.52 ± 0.10) compared to PN space.
source: Notably, while response vectors calculated from PN data were highly correlated (r=0.71 ± 0.08), such a correlation significantly decreased in the modelled KC space (r=0.52 ± 0.10; Student's t-test between r distributions of PN and KC data: p 0, n=4774), indicating that the signal transformation operated by the proposed MB neural architecture induces a strong decorrelation among odour signatures.
evidence: The Results section reports correlation values with statistical test.

claim: The MB neural architecture induces strong decorrelation among odour signatures.
source: Notably, while response vectors calculated from PN data were highly correlated (r=0.71 ± 0.08), such a correlation significantly decreased in the modelled KC space (r=0.52 ± 0.10; Student's t-test between r distributions of PN and KC data: p 0, n=4774), indicating that the signal transformation operated by the proposed MB neural architecture induces a strong decorrelation among odour signatures.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the correlation comparison.

claim: The model accounts for expansion of coding space from AL to MB, enhancing inter-stimuli decorrelation.
source: Moreover, it accounts for the expansion of the coding space from the AL to the MB (Lin et al., 2014; Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Stopfer, 2014), enhancing inter-stimuli decorrelation and confirming previous theoretical works based on artificial datasets (Olshausen and Field, 2004; Peng and Chittka, 2017).
evidence: The Results section states this model capability with citations to supporting literature.

claim: A trained MBON showed larger decrease in firing probability when presented with the CS than with an unfamiliar stimulus, demonstrating learning.
source: As expected, we found that a trained MBON showed a larger decrease in firing probability when presented with the CS than with the unfamiliar stimulus, demonstrating learning (Figure 5B).
evidence: The Results section reports this finding from model simulations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The model predicts weak learning in backward pairing (when US begins before CS).
source: Interestingly, the model predicts weak learning in the case of backward pairing – that is when US and CS are partially overlapping, but the US begins before the CS – whereas both early and delay conditioning predict strong learning, that is, a large CS-specific down-regulation of MBON firing probability (Figure 5B).
evidence: The Results section describes model predictions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both early and delay conditioning predict strong learning with large CS-specific down-regulation of MBON firing probability.
source: Interestingly, the model predicts weak learning in the case of backward pairing – that is when US and CS are partially overlapping, but the US begins before the CS – whereas both early and delay conditioning predict strong learning, that is, a large CS-specific down-regulation of MBON firing probability (Figure 5B).
evidence: The Results section describes model predictions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In trace conditioning, the model produced a down-modulation of MBON response that was shifted in time, appearing only after CS offset around the expected US arrival time.
source: Finally, in the case of trace conditioning, the model also produced a down-modulation of the MBON response. However, this learnt response was shifted in time: it appeared only after the CS offset, that is, around the US expected arrival time (Figure 5B).
evidence: The Results section describes model predictions for trace conditioning shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The model predicts that an MBON exposed to early protocol should learn to identify early components of the stimulus neural signature.
source: Stimulus representation is dynamic (see Figures 1 and 2). Hence, our model predicts that an MBON exposed to an early protocol should learn to identify the early components of the stimulus neural signature.
evidence: The Results section states this model prediction based on dynamic stimulus representation.

claim: The learned response occurs earlier in the early protocol than in the delay protocol (Wilcoxon test, p<0.001).
source: Indeed, the model shows that the learned response (a down-regulation of MBON firing probability) occurs earlier in the early than in the delay contingency (Wilcoxon test for non-parametric paired data, p<0.001; n=16) and with lower response latency variability (Barlett's test early vs delay, p<0.011; Figure 5D).
evidence: The Results section reports statistical comparison of model predictions shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The model predicts that trace conditioning should rely on identification of post-stimulus neural activity.
source: At the same time, it predicts that trace conditioning should rely on the identification of post-stimulus neural activity (Figure 5B).
evidence: The Results section states this model prediction.

claim: Backward conditioning led to scarce and unspecific responses in behavioral experiments, in agreement with model predictions.
source: In agreement with the model's predictions and previous reports (Felsenberg et al., 2014), backward conditioning led to scarce and unspecific responses (Figure 5E).
evidence: The Results section reports behavioral data shown in Figure 5E, comparing to model and literature.

claim: Positive ISIs of 1 or 4 seconds (early and delay protocols) induced specific memory formation with approximately 90 to 70% of trained bees showing conditioned responses to CS.
source: In contrast, positive ISIs of 1 or 4 s (early and delay protocols) induced specific memory formation (McNemar test, pbackward = n .s., pearly = 0.003, plate = 0.004), with ~90 to 70% of the trained bees showing conditioned responses to the CS and ~40% showing a generalised response to the unfamiliar stimulus during the test.
evidence: The Results section reports behavioral learning scores with statistical tests.

claim: Bees receiving reward 1 second after CS onset extended proboscis earlier and with less variability than those receiving reward towards the end of CS delivery.
source: Video tracking of the proboscis extension response showed that bees receiving the reward 1 s after CS onset extended the proboscis earlier and with less variability than those that received the reward towards the end of CS delivery (Kruskal-Wallis test, p=0.036; Barlett's test for data variance comparison, p=5e10–6; nearly = 26, ndelay = 20; Figure 5F).
evidence: The Results section reports behavioral measurements with statistical tests shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Bees exposed to trace conditioning showed weak and aspecific learning, highlighting the complexity of the task.
source: Finally, bees exposed to trace conditioning (ISI = 7 s) showed weak and aspecific learning - highlighting the complexity of the task (Dylla et al., 2013; Ito et al., 2008; Paoli et al., 2023a; Szyszka et al., 2011).
evidence: The Results section reports behavioral results with citations to related studies.

claim: In trace conditioning, learners showed PER latency comparable to the delay group but with broader distribution.
source: However, in opposition to the model's prediction, the learners showed a PER latency comparable to the delay group (Kruskal-Wallis test, p=0.992) but with a broader distribution (Barlett's test for data variance comparison, p=0.007; ndelay = 20, ntrace = 31).
evidence: The Results section reports behavioral measurements with statistical tests, noting discrepancy with model.

claim: Removing stable excitatory or inhibitory response profiles or short excitatory responses alone did not affect the difference in response timing between early and delay protocols.
source: Interestingly, removing stable excitatory or inhibitory response profiles or short excitatory responses alone did not affect the difference in response timing between protocols.
evidence: The Results section reports findings from model manipulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: Combined removal of inhibitory and short excitatory responses prevented the difference in MBON response latency between early and delay protocols.
source: Conversely, the combined removal of inhibitory and short excitatory responses from the odorant response patterns prevented the difference in MBON response latency between protocols.
evidence: The Results section reports findings from model manipulations.

claim: Reducing richness in glomerular response dynamics by removing early excitatory responses and delayed inhibition increases temporal stability of neural representation and prevents differential response latency between protocols.
source: In conclusion, reducing the richness in glomerular response dynamics by removing early excitatory responses and delayed inhibition increases the temporal stability of the neural representation of an olfactory stimulus and prevents the differential response latency observed between early and delay conditioning protocols.
evidence: The Results section concludes this from the model manipulation experiments.

claim: A simple but biologically realistic MB neural network model simulating essential aspects of MB connectivity can process real neurophysiological input and generate robust predictions that agree with empirical observations.
source: Our results show that a simple but biologically realistic MB neural network model simulating essential aspects of MB connectivity can process real neurophysiological input and generate robust predictions that agree with empirical observations.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: Excitatory responses occurred earlier than inhibitory ones and exhibited smaller temporal variability.
source: Excitatory responses occurred earlier than inhibitory ones and exhibited a smaller temporal variability.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes findings from the latency analysis.

claim: Excitation of PNs occurs in a single wave upon cholinergic input from OSNs to glomeruli with minor contribution of second-order excitatory local interneurons.
source: This suggests that excitation of PNs occurs in a single wave upon cholinergic input from the OSNs to the glomeruli of the antennal lobe, with a minor contribution – if any – of second-order excitatory local interneurons within the AL, which have been reported for Drosophila (Chou et al., 2010; Olsen et al., 2007) but so far not for honey bees (Girardin et al., 2013; Krofczik et al., 2008; Schäfer and Bicker, 1986).
evidence: The Discussion interprets the latency findings with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Lateral inhibition within the AL is responsible for triggering PN inhibition and terminating early excitatory responses.
source: On the other hand, inhibitory PN responses and the termination of early excitatory PN responses occurred within the same time window, approx. 40 ms after the onset of excitatory responses, suggesting that lateral inhibition within the AL is responsible for triggering PN inhibition and terminating early excitatory responses (see Figure 2, groups 7 and 8).
evidence: The Discussion interprets the temporal relationship of responses.

claim: Almost 50% of PN responses recorded contain an inhibitory component, underlining the dominant role of inhibitory AL interneurons.
source: Notably, we observed that almost 50% of PN responses recorded contain an inhibitory component (see Figure 2A, groups 1–3, 5, 7, 8), underlining the dominant role of inhibitory AL interneurons in shaping odour trajectories in the glomerular space.
evidence: The Discussion emphasizes this quantitative finding from the data.

claim: The findings contrast with previous calcium imaging analyses where only 2–10% of responses had an inhibitory nature but are coherent with electrophysiological recordings.
source: These observations are in contrast with previous calcium imaging analyses, where only 2–10% of responses had an inhibitory nature (Krofczik et al., 2008; Szyszka et al., 2005), but coherent with electrophysiological recordings showing a rich response diversity and prominence of inhibitory activity (Wilson et al., 2004).
evidence: The Discussion compares findings to previous studies with citations.

claim: In the honey bee AL, glomerular responses are modulated mainly by a local inhibitory network, unlike Drosophila where both local inhibitory and excitatory interneurons contribute.
source: Differently from Drosophila, where both local inhibitory and excitatory interneurons contribute to the olfactory tuning (Chou et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2010; Shang et al., 2007; Yaksi and Wilson, 2010), our analysis indicates that, in the honey bee AL, glomerular responses are modulated mainly by a local inhibitory network.
evidence: The Discussion contrasts findings with Drosophila literature.

claim: Almost 50% of all PN responses displayed either prolonged post-stimulus activity or a change in response direction after stimulus termination.
source: Almost 50% of all PN responses in our database displayed either a prolonged post-stimulus activity (see Figure 2, groups 2 and 6) or a change in response direction after stimulus termination (groups 3, 5, 7, 8).
evidence: The Discussion summarizes findings about post-stimulus activity.

claim: Post-stimulus activity results in recruitment of an offset-specific population of KCs that creates a neural image of the post-odour in the MB.
source: This results in the recruitment of an offset-specific population of KC – both in our model and in the literature (Ito et al., 2008; Lüdke et al., 2018) – that creates a neural image of the post-odour in the MB.
evidence: The Discussion describes this finding from model and cites supporting literature.

claim: The post-odour representation is different from the neural image of the odorant itself and provides a stable, slowly decaying after-image that is stimulus-specific.
source: Thus, the post-odour representation is different from the neural image of the odorant itself and provides a stable, slowly decaying after-image, which is stimulus-specific and temporally associated with the neural correlate of the odorant itself.
evidence: The Discussion characterizes the post-odour representation based on findings.

claim: The model predicts that after-stimulus signature of an odorant is more distinct and stable across time in the MB than in the AL.
source: Our modelling analysis predicts that the after-stimulus signature of an odorant is more distinct and stable across time in the MB than in the AL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Discussion states this model prediction with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: The duration of post-odour neural signature is about 10–15 seconds, compatible with the duration of CS/US gap in trace learning experiments.
source: Interestingly, the duration of the post-odour neural signature reported by us and by previous studies (Galili et al., 2011; Patterson et al., 2013; Szyszka et al., 2011) is about 10–15 s. As such, it is compatible with the duration of the CS/US gap in trace learning experiments (Galili et al., 2011; Paoli et al., 2023a; Szyszka et al., 2011; Wystrach et al., 2020), suggesting the possibility of its implication in this form of learning.
evidence: The Discussion relates findings to trace learning with citations.

claim: Differentiation between CS and novel odorant was observable in the model whenever CS anticipated US (ISIs of +1s and +4s) but less successful in backward and trace protocols.
source: A simulation of the action potential probability of an MBON after olfactory conditioning revealed that differentiation between the CS and a novel odorant was observable whenever the CS anticipated the US (ISIs of +1 s and +4 s) but less successful in the backward (ISI of –2 s) and trace protocols (ISI of 7 s).
evidence: The Discussion summarizes model simulation results.

claim: A learning window placed closer to stimulus onset (early protocol) resulted in early and temporally precise MBON responses.
source: However, the model predicts a difference in response latency and latency variability depending on relative CS/US arrival (ISI of +1 or+4 s): a learning window placed closer to stimulus onset (early protocol) resulted in early and temporally precise MBON responses, whereas a delayed learning window produced a similar learning score, but with higher response latencies and temporal uncertainty.
evidence: The Discussion describes model predictions about response timing.

claim: Experimental results confirmed model predictions showing early and delay protocols yielded comparable learning scores but differed in CS latency and precision.
source: Experimental results based on the same odorants that were fed to the model confirmed the model's predictions. They showed that early and delay protocols yielded comparable results in terms of learning score and CS-specificity while differing in terms of CS latency and precision (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: The Discussion reports agreement between model and behavioral data.

claim: Associative learning occurs upon coincident detection of CS and US neural elements.
source: These observations support the idea that associative learning occurs upon coincident detection of the CS and US neural elements.
evidence: The Discussion interprets findings in terms of learning theory.

claim: Trace conditioning cannot be explained by simple temporal coincidence of reward system activation and KC pool recruited at odour offset.
source: Such a discrepancy in measured and predicted response latencies suggests that trace conditioning cannot be explained by the simple temporal coincidence of a reward system's activation and a pool of KC recruited at odour offset.
evidence: The Discussion infers this from the discrepancy between model and behavioral data.

claim: Higher order cognitive processes, possibly involving attention mediated by the serotonergic system, could contribute to prolonging memory trace of the conditioned stimulus in trace conditioning.
source: Thus, a higher order cognitive process, possibly involving attention mediated by the serotonergic system, could contribute in prolonging the memory trace of the conditioned stimulus (Paoli et al., 2023a; Zeng et al., 2023).
evidence: The Discussion proposes this explanation with citations to relevant studies.

claim: The model shows that time contingency can be naturally encoded because olfactory representation in KCs evolves through time in a deterministic fashion.
source: Our model shows that this time contingency can be naturally encoded simply because the olfactory representation in the KCs evolves through time in a deterministic fashion.
evidence: The Discussion explains the model's mechanism for encoding time contingency.

claim: What is learned during US presentation is the KC configuration of the CS at that particular time rather than the expected reward time.
source: Thus, what is learnt during the US presentation is the KC configuration of the CS at this particular time. In other words, the MBON learns which subpopulation of KC is active during reward arrival rather than the expected reward time.
evidence: The Discussion explains the learning mechanism in the model.

claim: The model captures experimental measurements of proboscis response latency in bees, which tend to respond earlier than the expected reward.
source: Remarkably, the model captures the experimental measurements of the proboscis response latency in bees, which indeed tend to respond earlier than the expected reward (Figure 5D and F).
evidence: The Discussion notes agreement between model and behavioral data.

claim: Local inhibition played a crucial role in shaping initial PN activity and defining odour trajectories in the glomerular space.
source: Our findings revealed that about 50% of glomerular responses had an inhibitory component and that local inhibition played a crucial role in shaping the initial PN activity and defining odour trajectories in the glomerular space.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes key findings about inhibition.

claim: The mushroom bodies enhance olfactory discrimination ability and stabilize the olfactory after-image, effectively prolonging the stimulus signature after odour offset.
source: Our analysis suggests that the mushroom bodies enhance olfactory discrimination ability and stabilise the olfactory after-image, effectively prolonging the stimulus signature after odour offset.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes model findings about MB function.

claim: The rules behind the neural model (random connectivity, feedback inhibition, and MBON plasticity) are sufficient to generate relevant predictions for associative learning upon different learning protocols.
source: The coherence between measured and predicted behavioural scores suggested that the rules behind this neural model – that is random connectivity, feedback inhibition, and MBON plasticity – are sufficient to generate relevant predictions for associative learning upon different learning protocols.
evidence: The Discussion concludes this from the agreement between model and behavioral data.

claim: The model's predictions are robust to noise and biological variability.
source: In addition, by testing the model against physiological recordings of different stimulations, we showed that the model's predictions are robust to noise and biological variability.
evidence: The Discussion states this conclusion from testing the model with multiple recordings.

claim: Similar principles may guide odour signal transformation at the MB level in appetitive associative learning across insects.
source: Because the model incorporates not only neural assumptions pertaining to the honey bee olfactory system but also to the fruit fly and locust olfactory systems, similar principles may guide odour signal transformation at the level of the MB in appetitive associative learning across insects.
evidence: The Discussion generalizes findings across insect species based on model design.

claim: Convergence but also differences can characterize functional architectures of olfactory systems in different insect species.
source: This generality does not apply, however, to the nature of odour reshaping by local interneurons observed in the AL of bees, which seems to differ from that occurring in flies, thus highlighting the fact that convergence, but also differences, can characterise the functional architectures of olfactory systems in different insect species.
evidence: The Discussion concludes this from comparing findings across species.

claim: Calcium imaging recordings were conducted at 64x64 pixel resolution and approximately 127 Hz.
source: All images were acquired with a water immersion 16 x objective (Leica HC FLUOTAR 16 x/0.6 IMM CORR, Leica Microsystems, Germany), at 64x64 pixel resolution and ~127 Hz.
evidence: The Methods section specifies the imaging parameters used.

claim: Each KC is randomly innervated by approximately 7–10 PNs according to neuroanatomical studies in bees and flies.
source: Neuroanatomical studies in bees (Szyszka et al., 2005) and flies (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017; Caron et al., 2013) suggest that each KC is randomly innervated by approximately 7–10 PNs.
evidence: The Methods section cites neuroanatomical studies to justify model parameters.

claim: In the model, each KC receives connections from 30% of the input PN population.
source: Connections between PNs and KCs were modelled as pseudo-random, with each KC receiving connections 30% of the input PN population, as observed in bees (Szyszka et al., 2005) and flies (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017; Caron et al., 2013).
evidence: The Methods section describes model connectivity with citations.

claim: A synaptic plasticity threshold value of 15 was adopted for learning tests.
source: For the learning tests, a spt value of 15 was adopted.
evidence: The Methods section specifies the parameter value used.
